title: The King and the Beggar's Son (தமிழ்)
summary: Akbar boasts that every human being bows before his imperial majesty. Birbal introduces a little beggar boy who refuses to bow to pride. [TA]
keywords: the king and the beggar's son
full_text:
While walking through the grand bazaar of Agra disguised as ordinary merchants, Emperor Akbar observed thousands of citizens bowing, touching the earth, and shouting prayers of praise whenever his royal retinue passed. Back at the palace, Akbar felt a swell of pride and remarked to Birbal:

'Is it not glorious, Birbal? From the wealthiest merchant to the lowliest beggar, every single human being in Hindustan acknowledges my majesty and bows his head before me!'

Birbal smiled gently: 'Sire, men bow to your imperial power and your guards' spears. But respect of the soul cannot be commanded by a crown. There are souls in this city who bow only to truth and righteousness, not to mere royal robes.'

Akbar challenged him: 'Bring me one person in this capital who will not bow before my throne!'

The next morning, Birbal brought a seven-year-old beggar boy named Gopal into the Diwan-i-Khas. The child was dressed in clean, humble cotton, his eyes bright and completely unafraid.

Akbar had instructed the palace carpenter to lower the wooden lintel of the doorway so that anyone entering would be forced to bend their head and bow to pass through.

When the boy approached the doorway, he noticed the low beam. Instead of bending his head forward in a bow, the boy sat down on the floor, slid his feet through first, and crawled through on his back with his face turned toward the sky!

He stood up inside the hall, standing tall and looking directly into Akbar's eyes without trembling.

Akbar was intrigued: 'Boy, why did you crawl on your back instead of bowing your head to enter?'

Gopal replied with fearless simplicity: 'Sire, my mother taught me that a man should bow his head only before God, and before his parents and teachers who give him life and wisdom. If I had bowed merely to avoid a piece of wood, I would have surrendered my dignity to a carpenter's plank!'

Akbar was stunned by the child's courage and philosophical clarity. He looked at Birbal with deep humility:

'You were right, Birbal. True nobility of spirit is born in the heart, not on a throne.' Akbar granted the boy a scholarship at the imperial madrasa, ensuring he received the finest education in the realm.
moral: நீதி மற்றும் வாழ்க்கை பாடம்: Wit beats power
